newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong coffers brimming as handover looms.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong coffers brimming as handover looms.

text.p: Hong Kong Financial Secretary Donald Tsang unveiled coffers overflowing with cash on Wednesday but resisted any temptation to indulge in a spending spree in his last budget speech under British rule.

Tsang, who had to contend with China looking over his shoulder when he drafted the 1997/98 budget for the transitional year, won mixed reviews when he opted for caution in the face of the momentous changes ahead.

Mindful of the historic significance of the occasion, he hammered home the political message that capitalism, not communism, would prevail when Hong Kong became a Special Administrative Region of China on July 1.
Tsang stressed China's promise that Hong Kong would remain fiscally autonomous and its pledge not to milk the wealthy community of six million people of a single cent.
His budget speech was widely forecast to be conservative but expectations that he would unveil a huge windfall surplus had fuelled hopes of tax cuts.

Tsang said Hong Kong, where annual per capita gross domestic product of US$24,500 exceeds that of Britain, would begin its new era as part of China cushioned by more than HK$330 billion (US$42.7 billion) in reserves in the bank.
Despite reporting a HK$15.1 billion budget surplus and forecasting more to come, Tsang merely tinkered with tax bands and allowances, to the disappointment of those looking for tax cuts.
Hong Kong's salaries tax rate remains at 15 percent and the corporate rate at 16.5 percent.

"It's really left me speechless. I'm still bemused at the boldness of his ability to stand up and tell us he's going to accumulate HK$90 billion in surplus over the next four years," said Marshall Byres, chairman of tax services at Ernst & Young in Hong Kong.
Big business applauded Tsang's prudence, but Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp lamented his tight grip on welfare spending.

"The 1997-98 budget always had the potential to be a difficult one, but consultation and cooperation (with China) has produced a result conservative in its approach, but acceptable to most in the community," said the chairman of the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce, James Tien.
Tien said the budget was well-executed and a "sound basis for confidence". But his was a minority voice.
"I think the size of the surplus is utterly obscene and I'm very, very mad just on that," said Emily Lau, an outspoken critic of the government's social policy.
"We are probably the richest place on earth and to think we have several hundred thousand people living from hand to mouth," she said.
"I've got nothing against the tax reduction on wine, that's fine. But I think we should also do something for the elderly."
Tsang cut duties on wine to 60 percent from 90 percent.
Tax experts said they were disappointed Tsang had failed to seize the opportunity to hone Hong Kong's competitive edge.

"In order to maintain our competitiveness, not just for the next year, but into the next millennium, we believe he should consider some sort of move, such as reduction of corporate profit tax," Christina Lam, tax partner of Arthur Andersen, told Reuters.
The budget, Tsang told the Legislative Council, was unique and designed "specially to meet the circumstances of 1997".
He called the outcome a model of cooperation with China but served warning that Hong Kong would march to its own financial drum beat after the handover.
Tsang, who will continue to serve as the financial chief under Hong Kong's post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa, said future budgets would be handled by Hong Kong alone.
"(China) had made clear that after June 30 the preparation of the annual budget will be a matter entirely for the Special Administrative Region."
He also served notice that democratic freedoms remained the cornerstone of Hong Kong's prosperity.

Tsang had earlier spoken out against China's plans to roll back some of Hong Kong's human rights laws after the handover, igniting speculation that his days in government service may be numbered. But he hammered home the message again.
"The free flow of information is the lifeblood of a modern service economy," Tsang said. "It leads to transparency and accountability in both the private and public sectors."
